SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Vic Dickenson
by Dan Morgenstern

Washington, D. C.
July 1976
Yeah.
But this was an affair that was advertised -- jam sessions -- you know.
Right. You know -- they were open to the public so to speak.
Yeah.
Yeah.

-- musicians -- that helped them to get their start you know -- just playing there. And to get stand too like Dixieland player -- (inaudible). And puts them really -- but people expect them to play this type of music, you know.
So they stuck with it. That's the kind of jobs they got then, you know --

Yeah. Now, yeah, it's always been interesting to me about you in a certain time in your career when you were playing like with Beth Shay (PHONETIC) and you played what some people might call Dixieland and -- I don't like the word anyway. And then you turn around and play with Lester and, you know --
Play with Eddie --
Right.
With three different kinds of (Inaudible).
Right. So, but did they try to
type cast you too and --
I was type casted but I was just Dixieland you know. But I like (unintelligible). I like playing any kind cause I like it -- I like it. So I don't discriminate on what type if it's good.
You can also -- well then you feel at home then in almost any kind of --
(Simultaneous conversation)
Yeah, it don't take me long to get feeling at home. I takes a little while I supposed. But maybe a couple of days. Try and get (unintelligible) feeling that there.
Yeah, it's the rhythm is different than --
Yeah, it is a little different, yeah.

You were like -- say in the first year -- you had your band with Billie Berg's (PHONETIC) and (inaudible) and that's a place that's become famous because Dizzy and Berg played there you know like the first time they did --
Yeah, a lot of guys played there. Hawkins did. I don't know for sure that Louis didn't play there. I'm not sure.
With a big band I guess at that
Vic Dickenson (Interviewed by Dan Morgenstern) - (1975):
I read somewhere that you started on organ, that you played organ.

Well, there was some organ, the old-time church organ... Before the congregation could afford a pipe organ. It was a pump organ, and people did (?) with their feet. And it's a large thing, with a few scales in it...
Was it in the house?
Yes. It belonged to my grandmother.
Did anybody in your family play?

I never heard my mother play, but they tell me that she used to play. I never did hear her play. But I heard my father play. He used to play violin. But he played like... I don't know what kind of tap(?) songs(?) they were, but they were reels or something. I think they were sort of like the reel, because some of them ...(?)...
Yes, that's a dance.
Yes. Those kind of songs he would play, like Irish things and... So I don't know... But he had a beautiful violin. He sure knew how to play it.
Would he let you touch his violin?
Yeah. Well, yes, I got to touch it. I liked to hear him play it, so I didn't do much to it.
You said once that you had been playing the instrument, but you hadn't thought about becoming a musician, which is a
Dickenson - 2
very different thing. How did that happen with you? players

Well, I was going to be a (?) contractor. That's what my father wanted me to be. So he had to start from the bottom. And from the bottom meant that you had to mix the sand and the mortar and stuff together. Then you had to carry it. And in those days they had laddering(?), like foot(?) ladder(?) stuff -- you had to learn that.

And I was carrying some mortar up on a scaffold, and the ladder...the rung on the ladder under my foot broke, with all this powder mixture on me, and it bent me backwards double nearly. I hurt my back; I sprained my back. Therefore, I couldn't do that any more. So I had to start...I started playing. Not very good at first, but... Still not very good.
But had you thought about it before that happened?

I liked playing. I liked music. Frankly, I was crazy about music from the start. Music, and also I wanted to be a cartoonist. I liked to draw things, you know. Not only just funny things; I liked to draw beautiful things, too. I thought they were kind of pretty when I'd draw them, but I guess they just looked like First Grade doodle drawings, heh-heh. But you know...
Have you still got any? Did you save any?
Hmm?
Dickenson - 3
Did you save any of your drawings?

No. One time they had a contest of the students in the school. We were trying to get the people to get us a new school, a junior high school. And they had a contest, a drawing contest for students that were drawing (?)... I don't know what you call it. Anyhow, I can't think of the words. They wanted to attract the people more than ...(?)... thing, and they wanted that junior high school, you know. I ...(?)... It wasn't much of a picture, I'll tell you.
You mean like a scholarship?
No. It was just... We got five dollars for winning the thing, you know, the student... And it was... Yes, it was having(?) its little boosters. It was a nice thing for me.
How old were you then?
I was in junior high. I guess I was in the seventh grade. How old would I be by then, in seventh grade? 13? 12 or 13, yeah...
12, yeah.
Let me see. I had to go through all the grades, so I never skipped none. Let me see. First, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh.... Seven and six is thirteen. I must have been thirteen...
Dickenson - 4
You were six when you started school?
Six... I was thirteen years old. 12 or 13.
The American system of grading.... I think about that, because I went through a different...
I was probably thirteen. I guess I must have been twelve and going onto thirteen; to end the year at thirteen.
How old were you when you went to work for your father?
Hmm?
Did you go to work for your father, Jerry, when you were still in school?
Did I work for my father when?
Like, while you were still in school.
Well, when I got in high school, that's when I worked; in the summertime, you know. That was during that period.
During the holidays.
Well, no, not during the holidays. Just a summer job, you know. ...(?)... to contract houses -- to plaster and all that, you know: that's what I was going to be.
He had his own business, then.
Yes. He was his own...
And that was in Xenia.
Dickenson - 5
Partly Xenia and partly Springfield, partly Columbus.
I was thinking about you when they had that hurricane.

Yes. Well, it ruined our house there. We had to destroy it, because it was too rickety to stand. But it's a funny thing, too. I had just put this aluminum cover over it, and all of that money got messed away. It's all re-done now. It's tough to put it on the ...(? )...(? )...
Who was living there then?
Oh, just my niece was there...was living there then. I had just gone, just about a year before -- my sister was living at the time. She died in ...(? )...
Were you the youngest?
Yes. I'm the youngest living. There were two younger than me, but they died years ago. Two girls who were younger. But now I only have one brother living, and he's in the hospital... And that's that.
Your brother who was a musician, was he a musician when you were kids?
No. He had other activities to do.
How much difference was there between you?
The one that you've seen in the picture?
Yes.

Three years. He couldn't have taught me. No, I taught my own self. I used to play with the records. We would get a new record about once a year, so in a whole year I could learn everything anybody played on it! You know? [LAUGHS]
What kind of records?

I liked the Mamie Smith records. Mamie Smith and the Jazz Hounds. And...oh, there was quite a... Fletcher Henderson at the piano and... I used to listen to every instrument, you know. I was very interested in the way they sounded.
You had a trombone then?

Yeah, there was a trombone in my house. My brother used to play on it, yeah. I had another brother that used to play on it. And he stopped playing on it, found something else to do. So I would pick it up now and then and play with the record; you know, just try and play what I heard.
You said you got a new record about once a year. So playing the phonograph wasn't much of... You just happened to have a phonograph that was not being used all the time.
Yeah...
It was like something that...
Dickenson - 7
Well, once in a while we'd get a new record, you know. I used to like the... There was a band called (?)'s Black Aces. I used to like that band. That was a good band.
Do you know who made some records with them?
No.
Miff Mole. Those are his first records.

You're kidding. I always liked Miff Mole. I thought he was a beautiful trombone player. And he did... He used to play some beautiful trombone. But I guess he lost that... He got very sick, and when you get sick, you can't expect a person to play like they did when they were feeling their greatest. And I guess a lot of people don't understand that.
Well, they...
But they all find out if they live long enough. Heh-heh. You can't do anything at your greatest all the time! Well, I guess you have to live and find out.
They want a musician to be like a machine that can compete...
Right. And never break down.
Right. Well, they just don't understand very much about what...
But there's a lot of people like that, you know.
They don't really understand music. It depends on how you feel and it depends on how you are, too.
Right.
It's a different thing... Anyway, listening to the phonograph was... I don't think maybe there would have been any music like it happened if it hadn't been that records came out just about that time.

Yeah. Records did... But I'll tell you, I used to like to watch minstrel shows when they used to come in town. I used to like to watch the parades. They used to have a parade, and the guys would have tall silk hats on with dusters. I don't know if you know about a duster. It's a coat...a gingham coat or something like that, that they would put on to keep the dust off of them riding them horses and... In them days was horse-and-buggy days, you know. And they were (?)ing down the street, parading there. And I used to like to hear the band. The bands played just Jazz. Just Jazz, but marching Jazz. You see, there's a difference in marches. Marches can be jazzy if you want it to be.
Like what they call a quick step and that sort of thing?
Dickenson - 9

I don't know what sort of step they call it, but... You know, I could say [SINGS SOUSA THEME, WITHOUT SYNCOPATION]. Now, the way these guys would say it: [SINGS IT WITH SYNCOPATIONS AND BROKEN RHYTHMS]. It's the same marching tempo, but it's a struttin' tempo. You dig?
Mmm-hmm. That swings, too.
Yeah, it's a swingin'... And them bands would play like that. You know, they wouldn't play it just... And I call that Jazz.
Where did you see those bands?
They used to come to our town, minstrel shows, you know... And I used to like to see them.
What was a show like that like? What would there be?
Like various comedians and things. Minstrel shows, you know. And they had a guy called... Mister Something. Oh, what was his name? Mister Bones. All that stuff.
So it was still strictly a minstrel thing.
It was minstrel. It was a minstrel. There was no Jazz them days.
Would there be like things that would stand out? Like, they would have a very good band...
Well, I liked that music. That's the main thing that ...(?)..., yeah.
Dickenson - 10
So there were good musicians in those days.
Well, they sounded good to me.
Were you aware at that time... Did people think that there was a music called Jazz? Or was that just something that came out on a record label? Or was there...
I don't really know where the word "Jazz" comes from.
But in other words, people didn't refer to it as that.
Huh?
When there was a music that we now call Jazz, or some things that came before that... What was it called? Or was it called anything?
Ragtime.
Oh, Ragtime. Right.
Yeah, Ragtime. I guess that was called Ragtime probably, you know.
What they were playing in the Minstrel shows.
Yeah. I guess that was called Ragtime.

But then when you would hear marching bands and things, or you would hear music on the records, like the Mamie Smith thing, did you make a distinction between all those and say that this seemed like a different kind of music? Or did it all...
Dickenson - 11

It was kind of a Blues thing, you know. I guess people have always had Blues singers... I don't know. I guess every people that's oppressed and... Way deep in their mind, they have a Blues or a Church piece they think of. And all Church pieces give me the blues. They do. I don't know, but they make me feel sorta bluish. I don't know what it is. It's this heartstring pulling thing. That's why I don't like to play Church numbers in a Jazz spot, because I get despondent. Do you understand?
Yes.

I can play the Blues. I don't get despondent with the Blues. But with Church music I get very despondent. You know? I just don't... There's a thing about that. I get... Well, I was raised, and people used to play these pieces and sing these numbers, you know. It makes me think about them so much, you know. And I don't like to get that way when I'm in a nightclub, playing -- you know?
Yes.
I don't know what it is.
Well, the Blues expresses a different kind of feeling(?)...
The Blues is a different thing to me... I can play the Blues all day long. The Blues... A lot of is
Dickenson - 12

like you're jammin', you know. But if you're playing a Church number that I've been raised on all the time for Church especially, that's when I really get the blues. I get very despondent. You know what I mean? So that's my ...(?). . .(?). . .
In your home town you didn't have the kind of funeral parades like they had in New Orleans?
No, we didn't have that.
That's a different attitude.
Yes, it is.
You can play those things, like "A Closer Walk With Thee".
I didn't have any of that...
Like jumping...
Yeah, but see, I didn't have that. Everything I had was so sort of subtle (?).
What denomination were your people?

We were Methodist. That's a different... Those numbers seem so valuable to me. They're (?) to be played at places, at a place of that sort. It took me years to be able to...or to convince myself to try to play "When The Saints Go Marching In." It took me years. But not so with this other number...what's that other number...? There's another number.
Dickenson - 13
"A Closer Walk With Thee"?

"A Closer Walk." That didn't effect me as "The Saints" did. But there was a guy that really started "The Saints", really started that song to be very popular as a Jazz song, and he was an (you know, what do you call the guys who get...?) evangelist. And he came to my home town. His name was Reverend Beckon. And he used to have a Jazz group that went with him. And they used to play "When The Saints Go Marching In." And that's when the people really started catching on to "When The Saints Go Marching In." Around '24 or '25...no, about '26, I would think. His name was Reverend Beckton. In fact, he got murdered in Philadelphia by gangsters or something.
How did you spell his last name?

Beckton. He's the first one that I can recall (I mean, in this part of the country) who started that on "When The Saints Go Marching In", rolling(?)... He had a Jazz band with him, that traveled with him. He was an evangelist, like Billy Graham. I think Billy Graham has got a band...
He's got Ethel Waters. He had her for a long time.
Yeah, oh yeah.
Which is quite something to have. I don't know how she sounds now, but...
Dickenson - 14
I think he's got a band with him, too, hasn't he?
Yeah, well, he must have. He's got the singers, something to back him up.
Well, a lot of them ...(?)...
Did this Reverend Beckton travel all over the country?
He traveled around, too, yeah. Then he got to be in Philadelphia for a little while, and that's where he met his end.
He must have been on to something good.
I don't know.
Where did you first hear the Blues, that you knew it was the Blues?

I don't know really. But I listened to the words of the Blues then. It was Mamie Smith I used to listen to, and Bessie Smith...and Trixie Smith, yeah... And there were some other Smiths then, too. There was a lot of Smiths...
Clara.
Clara, yeah. Just a gang of them.
They were not related.
They weren't related. But you know, everybody was named Smith them days. Smith, Johnson or Jones. [LAUGHS]
Dickenson - 15
Don't you think we'd better eat?
Well, you're the cook. You know when.
Well, let me see if ...(?)... everything's hot and ...(?)...
[PAUSE]
You don't like that.
Yeah, I do. But it's sipping, you know...
Yeah. Well, that's what it is. It's called a ..(?).. tizzy(?).
Mmm.
Tizzy-tazzy. Heh-heh.
Where were we?
I don't know...
Well, we were really talking about when you picked up the trombone...
[ETC., AS THEY MOVE AND MR. DICKENSON COUGHS SEVERAL TIMES; COMMENTS ON BASEBALL GAME ON THE TELEVISION]
Baseball is such a beautiful game. You to ...(?)... play fair and not let anybody catch up with you.
[ETC., PAUSE]
So what else did you want to talk about?
Well, let's see where we were. We were talking about Blues, and when you first... You said that when you started to play as a professional, that you had played with some
Dickenson - 16
bands before that.

Well, I didn't make any money, you know, just... At the first gig I ever made, I think I made 50 cents or something. But I kind of liked it, you know. I liked that. Of course, in retrospect(?)... I wanted to be a comedian, too. That was another ambition I had.
A comedian?

Mmm-hmm. But I out-grew that. I just loved comedians. I loved the way they did things, you know. And you didn't know they were the next day because they had their makeup on. That's the way I wanted it to be. I didn't want people to know who it was the next day! So that was another phase...
So after I hurt myself, you know, carrying that (?) that time...
How old were you then?

I was 17. I was already playing. My brother was a better musician than me at the time, because he could read and all. I didn't take no time up thinkin' about reading, you know. I just played, you know, whatever heard as the tonic note, which I had known... The tonic note, as I had known it, as Do -- you know, Do-Re-Me-Fa-Sol-La-Tee.
Right.
Dickenson - 17

So all I wanted to know was the tonic, you know, and then I would go from there. I used to like to sing in quartets and things, so I could always play the second... I could always play the second or third chorus just by hearing it.
By ear.

Yeah. So I worked out from there pretty well, until I finally got a job... I had joined the union in Columbus, Ohio, at the time. And the guy wrote in and asked...said he wanted a trombone player that could read. So the union came to me, and told me about it. And I said, "Well, I can't read." I said, "I can spell, but I can't read." [LAUGHS] Spelling, by that I meant I could do the Do-Re-Me thing. But if you said in the key of G and the key of D and the key of all them things, I didn't know what the heck you was talkin' about. You know? I knew what you was talkin' about, but I couldn't do it that way. I had to go from Do. So I told him, "I can't make it because I can't read like that." So he said, "Well, come on anyhow" -- they were stuck for somebody. So I said, "All right."

And I played a month. I had a beat-up trombone, and one of the guys in the band had a trombone for sale. The money was thirty-five dollars a week, and he wanted fifteen dollars a week for the trombone that he had... He had a
Dickenson - 18

...(?)... My trombone was beat. So he said he'd sell it to me. All I had to do was pay him, you know, each week, fifteen dollars a week. So that left me twenty dollars to pay my room and board with.
I had been there a month, and I got fired. I paid him the fifteen dollars... So anyway, I didn't have enough money to get home on.
Where were you? In Columbus?

No, I was in Madison, Wisconsin. I went from Columbus to Madison, Wisconsin. So I used to job around on the piano a little bit, you know... So that night, there was a drummer in town that said he had to have a piano player. He couldn't find nobody to play piano. And he asked me would I help him out. I said, 'Well, I can't play no piano; you know, just a few (?)s in the key of C on piano.' He said, 'That's all right.' So I went out there and did it.
How big a group was that?

Just me and the drummer. And they gave us a tip and everything, you know. So I made enough money to get back home. So at least I had a trombone. It was a used trombone, but it was a pretty good one. And a whole month of work shot! Heh-heh... But the guy didn't even let me know that I was being fired until the day that he told me.
Dickenson - 19
And that's the day that I didn't have to go to work no more. See what I'm saying?
Short notice.
Yeah.
What was the name of the band?

Don Phillips. That was a band from up in Columbus. Well, they came from Fort Wayne, Indiana. I remember working here in Madison, Wisconsin at this place called the Broadway Gardens. Anyway, they had a good trombone player who ...(? )... He could read and everything. (?)They let me go.(?) So then... That's when I decided I was going to learn to read. That made me learn to read -- and to write, too. That's when I started doing both. I just made up my mind I was going to do it. So I asked different questions from different people...
So you didn't go and study or anything.
No. I never had a lesson. Never had a lesson.
Not on the horn or anything.
Not on the horn. Not on anything. Except the (?) grammar school.
Did you have an opportunity then... While you were learning and so on, did you have an opportunity to play? Were there gigs you could pick up...?
Dickenson - 20
While I was doing what?
While you were... You said that made you decide to...
Sure. Yeah. I mean, I couldn't do anything else. There was no other kind of work for me to do.
Yeah.
So I took little gigs around there, you know. Then I had been with this group of guys from Columbus before, ...(?)., and we got a lot...you know... [LONGISH SILENCE]
So in a sense, you kind of came on the trombone by... well, by coincidence, because it happened to be there.
Yes.
But once that was there, then that was it. You didn't feel like you wanted to learn another instrument or something like that necessarily.
Well, yeah. But I mean, I kept trying to (?) the trombone, and... Because it seems to be so much...
Yeah, harder.

Yeah, well... You might think it's that. It sounds funny, but long ago a guy was telling me, 'If you want to learn your trombone, you've got to sleep with it.' So I used to put my trombone right under my bed every night, and sleep with it! I think that's got a lot of things to do with it, the psychology to that, you know. If you got your
Dickenson - 21
money on one thing, you'll make it if you keep your money and not (?)go anywhere(?).
In the bands at that time... You said he let you go because of your reading. Could the other guys in the band read?
Yeah, they could read. [INAUDIBLE SENTENCE]
Well, was that more or less common for most of the working bands then?

Yeah, a lot of them. I was beginning to learn to read. I just came around at a time where I didn't... They didn't ...(?)...(?)... about music, and I didn't... The only thing that I knew about music was Do-Re-Me-Fa-Sol-La-Ti-Do. You know? That's all I knew.
[MURKY SECTION FOLLOWS]

I mean, I knew E-G-B-D-F. Every (?) chord has (?). I knew that. One was the bass clef and one was the treble clef. Right? (?)Because you'll find all of them.(?) I knew that. One was the bass clef, one was the treble clef. Right? That's the line ...(?)...(?)... And that didn't occur to me that's what those words were. That's what ...(?)... And I should have paid it mind. Because I just didn't pay it any mind. I just went from "Where's (?)?" right on.
So there's a lot to be explained. In the beginning of any study, you should learn the very basic part of it.
Dickenson - 22

That's why I never learned Latin or Geometry, because I didn't learn the very basic, the very first thing you learn early on. And I was sick at the time when we had Geometry, I was sick when they had Latin. I was sick at the beginning of the class, of the year, and I was out of school. So I didn't learn any of it. There's a key to these things. There's a key to these things. There's a key to them all. And you get that first key to everything, then later you can unlock the door. Otherwise, you just go round and round by the way(?) to where you want to get. But if you do ever make it, you make it better than the guy that had the key in the first place. But you've made it the hard way. It's very aggravating that way. But some people are going to do it that way, do it the right way. The first guy that did it, he didn't have nobody teach him. You know? But he done it. Right?
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]
So what was the next band you went out with after that?

I went down to... Oh, I went with another band called Harry Stevens(?). But it was a very short engagement(?). So the next group, I would say, I went down to Lexington, Kentucky, to a band called Big Bill Smith's
Dickenson - 23

Band. He was a very big guy who played alto saxophone. And in the days before I got there, he had been pretty big guy, you know. He was around the same time as...oh, I'm trying to think of his name... Fess Williams. Do you know Fess Williams?
Mmm-hmm.

He was around the same time as Fess Williams, right there. Fess Williams was going pretty good there in New York ...(?), and he was going pretty good in there because ...(?). He had a small band, five or six pieces that ...(?).(?).
[INAUDIBLE]
Everybody knew about Fess Williams, in and out of Kentucky... Boy, he was a real champion, you know. [INAUDIBLE MONEY]
Well, he was making a lot of money, I guess.

He made good. I don't know if he made a lot of money, but he made a very good name for himself. Probably the kind of people ...(?). make a lot of money in ...(?).(?).(?). I'm not making a lot off money. Never did. But Fess had a big name going to ...(?).(?)., you know. I wouldn't say that he made an awful lot of money.
He was at the Savoy for a long time.
Yes, he was.
Dickenson - 24
He was like before the Savoy Sultans.

He had prestige, though, in his heyday. Everybody thought he was the greatest band in the world. But it didn't sell; it wasn't selling. I don't think anybody made a whole lot of money in them days. But it gave you prestige. It was a jumping-off point. You know?
So was Big Bill Smith the same kind of band as Fess Williams?
Sort of like that.
The same ...(? )...

Well, no, not too much. He didn't ...(? )... He was one of the first bands I had ever heard anywhere. Because I had seen people ...(? )...; you know what I mean, sort of playing for a dance or something. I remembered seeing him years ago. There used to be a band out of Wilberforce called The Wilberforcians, and that had... That was Horace Henderson's little group; they called themselves the Wilberforcians. And they used to come in town and play, too, you know -- in my town; this is Xenia. Then another band that used to come there was the Central(?) Synco Septet.
That's what became McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
That was McKinney's Cotton Pickers. But it was Central Sextet at first. It would have been a quintet.
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Vic Dickenson
by Dan Morgenstern

Washington, D. C.
July 1976
eb PROCEEDINGS
: -- this recording -- are you sure you're at the right place?
Yeah, that's the start of the (inaudible) there.
Oh. Was this right -- the volume?
It has no effect on the volume. Leave the volume high -- don't make the volume higher when you record.
Yeah, well on mine it doesn't make any difference (inaudible).

Yeah. Well, they're trying to sell that particular number or piece. But they're not thinking about their clients, who they're representing. They're likely representing cigarettes and beers, or this and that and the other. And those people that... There's a lot of people that won't listen to that channel just because; because that it sticks to one and it don't vary. You know?
During the times when the bands were on the air a lot...

I think those were great days. I think they should bring that back, and broadcast the bands from places that...certain nightclubs and things. People will be listening to that. I remember when I used to listen for the Cotton Club or for Roseland Ballroom or different things
Dickenson - 158
like that... Or this hotel or that hotel, the band... I knew what I wanted to hear, and I'd hear it. And the bands never played the same way either. They played a variety of numbers.
And you had so many different kinds of bands, too.
Yes. But those were good days. I think that should be brought back.
They had a lot of that music on because I guess people were dancing to it also.

But they were staying home listening to it a little bit, and then they could figure out whether they wanted to go the next night or something. If they wanted to go out, they'd say, 'Let's go hear this band. We've been listening to them at this place.' And yet they're still satisfying the people, and they're selling the commodities that they sell, you know. They're getting different people to listen to it, where they never would listen at all if it was the same old stuff. I've always been that way. And I wish I were a disk jockey; that's what I would do. I'd be playing them. That's the reason, I suppose, I would never get hired. I wouldn't play just one thing all of the time. Every day you hear the same thing. Which is terrible!
Yeah. Well, there are a few stations that are a little different. But the dominant thing is just one thing, yes.
Dickenson - 159
Yes.
Even though, you know, they tried recently, and they've been doing it for a while now...but bringing Country Music into...

That's all right, too. And so is Rock-and-Roll. But don't play nothin' but Rock-and-Roll. [SINGS FIFTIES JUMP REFRAIN LOUDLY] I mean, you know, it's all right to do it once or twice. But not every number. It's going to be fast, it's going to be slow, but it's going to be the same...generally the same things. Why don't they vary it?
Of course.

And don't play too much of any type, but give everybody a chance to hear something. Some people like to hear pretty music, beautiful music, you know. I can stand listening to any type of music played once, one piece, one thing. But if you're going to keep cramming it down my throat, every number I hear is the same thing, I'm going to turn that off.
No, it's very monotonous. Was there any... Were bands broadcasting locally, too? In other words, if you were working with Speed Webb, was there any broadcasting?
We broadcasted a few times. Sure, we did. But it wasn't on a national hookup, but around the town and
Dickenson - 160

around the vicinity. But we just didn't get a chance. We didn't get a chance to make records or anything. That's why that band wasn't a success. We didn't make records. And we didn't come to New York.
That was important, coming to New York.
Yes, it was very important.
Why was that?
Well, they said you're not made until you come to New York in them days. I don't know if they still say that yet. I think they do.
In a way, yes.
If you're not made, then you go to New York!
So a lot of bands never made it to New York, and some got here and didn't do so well...
Well, yes... But they did give it a try. But we didn't.
There were some great bands, like McKinney's Cotton Pickers, that never seemed to work New York much, I guess.
But they did come to New York. They did come to New York, see. They were out in Detroit. They were talked about. But they had to come to New York to make records in the first place, you see.
That was a pretty good band, wasn't it?
What?
Dickenson - 161
McKinney's.
Oh yeah. It was a wonderful band. Yes! Some good guys in there. There was... For a while they had Benny Carter, and they had Don Redman.
That's two pretty fair arrangers and saxophonists.
Yeah. You can say that again.
Yeah, Redman tends to be sort of ignored as a player, but he was pretty nifty.
He wrote some good songs. He wrote 'How Am I Doin?' 'Save It Pretty Mama.' Just a gang of songs.
'Gee, Baby.'
'Gee, Baby, Ain't I Good To You.' 'Save It Pretty Mama'...

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Copyright notice and interview heading
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warning and the Smithsonian heading for Dan Morgenstern's July 1976 interview with Vic Dickenson.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Dixieland typecasting and playing in different styles
segments.summary: Dickenson says he was typecast as a Dixieland player but likes any good music and feels at home in a new style within a couple of days; Morgenstern mentions his band at Billy Berg's.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Pump organ, his father's violin and music at home
segments.summary: He recalls his grandmother's pump organ, his mother who reportedly played, and his father's beautiful violin playing of reels and Irish tunes.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Training to be a contractor and the ladder accident that led to music
segments.summary: His father wanted him to be a plastering contractor; a broken ladder rung sprained his back and he turned to playing.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Wanting to draw cartoons and the school drawing contest
segments.summary: He loved music but also wanted to be a cartoonist, won five dollars in a junior-high drawing contest, and works out his age at the time.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Summer work for his father and his family in Xenia
segments.summary: He worked summers for his father's contracting business around Xenia, Springfield and Columbus; the storm that ruined the family house; his siblings.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Teaching himself by playing along with records
segments.summary: He taught himself by playing along with records such as Mamie Smith and the Jazz Hounds, using a trombone his brothers had left in the house.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Miff Mole's early records and how illness affects a musician
segments.summary: He liked Black Aces records and Miff Mole, and says a sick musician cannot play at his best and audiences expect machines.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Minstrel shows and marching bands in his home town
segments.summary: He loved the minstrel shows and parades with bands playing syncopated marches, which he calls jazz.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: What the music was called before jazz
segments.summary: He does not know where the word jazz came from; the music of the minstrel shows was called ragtime.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Why church music makes him despondent and the blues does not
segments.summary: He can play the blues all day but church pieces from his upbringing make him despondent, so he avoids them in nightclubs.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Methodist upbringing and no funeral parades at home
segments.summary: His home town had no New Orleans style funeral parades; his family was Methodist and it took years before he would play The Saints.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Reverend Beckton and When the Saints Go Marching In
segments.summary: An evangelist, Reverend Beckton, travelled with a jazz band and popularised The Saints around 1926, and was later murdered in Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: First hearing the blues: Mamie, Bessie, Trixie and Clara Smith
segments.summary: He listened to the words of the blues singers named Smith, none of whom were related.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Break for dinner and baseball
segments.summary: They stop to eat, watch a baseball game, and Morgenstern steers back to when Dickenson started professionally.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: First gigs, the wish to be a comedian, and playing by ear at 17
segments.summary: He earned about 50 cents at his first gig, once wanted to be a comedian, and at 17 played by ear using only the tonic note.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: The union job for a reading trombonist and buying a used trombone
segments.summary: The Columbus union sent him to a band wanting a trombonist who could read; he bluffed, paid a bandmate fifteen dollars a week for a trombone, and was fired after a month.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Stranded in Madison, a piano gig, and deciding to learn to read
segments.summary: Fired by the Don Phillips band in Madison, Wisconsin, he earned his fare home playing piano with a drummer and resolved to learn to read and write music.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Never a lesson, and picking up small gigs
segments.summary: He never had a lesson on anything, took small gigs while learning, and came to the trombone more or less by coincidence.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Sleeping with the trombone and the lack of basic training
segments.summary: He was told to sleep with the trombone, admits he never learned the basics of reading, and reflects that you need the first key to unlock a subject.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Big Bill Smith's band in Lexington and the Fess Williams comparison
segments.summary: After a short stint with Harry Stevens he joined Big Bill Smith's band in Lexington, which Dickenson compares to Fess Williams's band and prestige.

segments.chapter: Boyhood and learning the trombone
segments.title: Visiting bands in Xenia: the Wilberforcians and the Synco Septet
segments.summary: The first bands he heard in Xenia included Horace Henderson's Wilberforcians and the Synco Septet that became McKinney's Cotton Pickers.

segments.title: New session heading and adjusting the tape recorder
segments.summary: A new heading for the July 1976 session and talk about recorder volume settings.

segments.title: Written arrangements, heads and copying solos in the early bands
segments.summary: Early bands used a mix of written parts and heads, each thought its own style the best, and players copied each others' solos.

segments.chapter: Early Midwest bands (first typescript)
segments.title: Television chatter before continuing

segments.chapter: Early Midwest bands (first typescript)

segments.title: What he would like to record: his own group and arrangers
segments.summary: He would choose his own players, tunes and arrangers and want the arranger to weigh his suggestions.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Bandleaders' faults and musicians' faults
segments.summary: Asked about leaders, he declines to name anyone but says both leaders and musicians can be aggravating.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's stars and why big bands cannot feature everyone
segments.summary: Asked about Louis's complaint that Henderson did not feature him, Dickenson says a big band full of stars cannot distribute solos and lists Henderson's players.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Kaiser Marshall's hand cymbal
segments.summary: He recalls Kaiser Marshall's exciting playing with a hand cymbal beaten with a stick.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Seeing the Henderson band in Ohio and Buster Bailey
segments.summary: He always went to see the Henderson band in Ohio because he and Buster Bailey were pals.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Rex Stewart, Earl Hines and who gets remembered
segments.summary: He wonders why no one mentions Rex Stewart, a great trumpet player, and they discuss how leaders get remembered.

segments.chapter: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
segments.title: Hot Lips Page and unremembered players
segments.summary: Lips Page is another unmentioned player, and Dickenson compares forgotten musicians to a worn-out discarded toy.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Pop Monroe's and Lester Young in 1932
segments.summary: At Pop Monroe's a pitcher of whiskey cost fifty cents; Lester sounded the same then; dinner is nearly ready.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Frankie Trumbauer's Tiger Rag solo and playing on changes
segments.summary: They discuss Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo that saxophonists admired, and that playing on changes was around early.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Few new records and listening to them on the road
segments.summary: Ten new records a month was a lot then; he could not afford a phonograph on the road and listened when at home.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Fans who listened as well as danced
segments.summary: There were fans in the late 1920s who invited musicians home and listened as well as danced.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Playing for dances: tempo and the dancers' feet
segments.summary: Dance tempos stayed fixed because the shuffling feet held a rushing drummer back, and good dancers influenced his playing.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Blanche Calloway fronting the band and who played in it
segments.summary: Blanche Calloway fronted the band for dances and theatres but did not write the arrangements; he lists members such as Clarence Smith, Abie Baker, Slim Moore and Stump Brady.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Hearing the teenage Art Tatum at the blind school in Columbus
segments.summary: A pianist took him to a Columbus blind school to hear a 14 or 15-year-old he calls the greatest piano player in the world, who played as well with either hand.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Teddy Wilson and Roy Eldridge in Speed Webb's band
segments.summary: Teddy Wilson already showed something in Speed Webb's band, and Roy Eldridge played fast like Rex Stewart with his own ideas.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Louis Armstrong telling a story with one note
segments.summary: Everybody was listening to Louis, who could swing people with a single note; Dickenson remembers his solo behind a blues singer on record.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Sunday jam sessions on 52nd Street
segments.summary: Mel Gabler's Sunday afternoon sessions were among the first advertised, open jam sessions, unlike the casual Harlem sessions.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Dixieland typecasting and playing in different styles
segments.summary: Dickenson says he was typecast as a Dixieland player but likes any good music and feels at home in a new style within a couple of days.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Billy Berg's club and who played there
segments.summary: Morgenstern mentions Dickenson's band at Billy Berg's, where Hawkins, Dizzy and Charlie played.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Slim Gaillard and Slam Stewart
segments.summary: They talk about Slim Gaillard as a dependable but unpredictable entertainer, and Slam Stewart's teaching and reunion with Benny Goodman.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Leo Watson and the Spirits of Rhythm
segments.summary: They compare Slim Gaillard to Leo Watson, a trombonist who mainly sang and kept Dickenson laughing; Morgenstern praises his As Long As I Live.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: The Lester Young record date and illness with pneumonia and ulcer
segments.summary: He made records with Lester in California and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Tired of one-nighters and leaving the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: He is fed up with travel and one-nighters, and left the World's Greatest Jazz Band partly for his legs and the grind of tours.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Learning to cook
segments.summary: He learned cooking by watching his mother, sister and wife and prefers his own home cooking to restaurants.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Travelling by bus, train and touring car then and now
segments.summary: Air travel is best now; in the Twenties bands crowded into touring cars with celluloid curtains, bass drum on the back and bad roads.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Dances and ballrooms like the Indiana Roof with Speed Webb
segments.summary: Bands played dances rather than concerts, sometimes in ballrooms like the Indiana Roof, where Speed Webb's jumping band played a few weeks.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Gus Wilson and the Speed Webb band personnel
segments.summary: They wonder what became of arranger-trombonist Gus Wilson and name Reunald Jones and Speed Dunn among the band.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Speed Webb's Midwest travel and the trip to Boston
segments.summary: The Webb band travelled mostly in the Midwest and went to Boston on an awful bus, still better than cars.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Hard to get location jobs for black bands
segments.summary: Landing a steady location like Roseland or the Grand Terrace was an important breakthrough and very hard for black bands.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Contact between black and white musicians and integration
segments.summary: Contact between the races began to improve in the late Twenties; the real change in the music came around 1935-36 with Dizzy and Parker, and integrated bands today work better.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Singin' the Blues, Trumbauer and Red Nichols
segments.summary: Trumbauer's Singin' the Blues solo was pretty and original; he also liked Red Nichols's bands, a different jazz from Fletcher Henderson's.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Miff Mole, Teagarden and Jimmy Harrison
segments.summary: Black and white players traded ideas; Miff Mole was the talk of the music world, and Teagarden and Harrison took their approach from Louis.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Bix Beiderbecke versus Red Nichols
segments.summary: They discuss why Trumbauer's solo stuck in people's minds and why Bix was idolised over Red Nichols, though Dickenson hears only similarity.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo and playing on changes
segments.summary: They discuss Trumbauer's rhythm, his Tiger Rag solo that saxophonists admired, and that playing on changes was around early.

segments.title: Few new records and listening to them on the road
segments.summary: Ten new records a month was a lot then; he could not afford a phonograph on the road and listened when at home.

segments.summary: There were fans in the late 1920s who invited musicians home and listened as well as danced.

segments.title: Playing for dances: tempo and the dancers' feet
segments.summary: Dance tempos stayed fixed because the shuffling feet held a rushing drummer back, and good dancers influenced his playing.

segments.chapter: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
segments.title: Blanche Calloway fronting the band and who played in it
segments.summary: Blanche Calloway fronted the band for theatres and dances but did not write the arrangements; he lists members such as Clarence Smith, Abie Baker, Slim Moore and Stump Brady.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Hearing the teenage Art Tatum at the blind school in Columbus
segments.summary: A pianist took him to a Columbus blind school to hear a 14 or 15-year-old he calls the greatest piano player in the world, who played as well with either hand.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Teddy Wilson and Roy Eldridge in Speed Webb's band
segments.summary: Teddy Wilson already showed something in Speed Webb's band, playing on the order of Earl Hines, and Roy Eldridge played fast like Rex Stewart with his own ideas.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Louis Armstrong telling a story with one note
segments.summary: Everybody was listening to Louis, who could swing people with a single note; Dickenson remembers his solo behind a blues singer on record.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Sunday jam sessions on 52nd Street
segments.summary: Milt Gabler's Sunday afternoon sessions were among the first advertised, open jam sessions, unlike the casual Harlem sessions.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Being typecast as a Dixieland player and playing in different styles
segments.summary: Sessions could stamp a player as Dixieland; Dickenson played with Bechet, Lester and Eddie Heywood, likes any good music and feels at home in a couple of days.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Billy Berg's club and who played there
segments.summary: Morgenstern mentions Dickenson's band at Billy Berg's in Los Angeles, where Hawkins, Dizzy and Charlie played.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Slim Gaillard and Slam Stewart
segments.summary: They talk about Slim Gaillard as a dependable but unpredictable entertainer, and Slam Stewart's teaching and reunion with Benny Goodman.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Leo Watson, Scatman Crothers and the Spirits of Rhythm
segments.summary: Dickenson recorded with Scatman Crothers and Leo Watson, a trombonist who mainly sang and kept him laughing; Morgenstern praises Leo's As Long As I Live.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: The Lester Young record date and illness with pneumonia and ulcer
segments.summary: He made records with Lester in California for Norman Granz and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.

segments.title: Tired of one-nighters and leaving the World's Greatest Jazz Band

segments.title: Leo Watson and the Spirits of Rhythm

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)

segments.summary: He made records with Lester in California and then got sick with pneumonia twice and an ulcer, which kept him out of playing for a while.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Tired of one-nighters and leaving the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: He is fed up with travel and one-nighters, left the World's Greatest Jazz Band partly for his legs, and hopes the band gets a steady gig.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Young players coming up: Warren Vache
segments.summary: Young players should get road experience; he predicts the not-yet-20 Warren Vache will be one of the big ones, and the music's core will remain.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: What Dixieland means: syncopated marches
segments.summary: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were mostly marches jazzed up with syncopation into strutting music, different from ragtime.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: What bands played when he started: songs and blues
segments.summary: Early bands played songs like Japanese Sandman and blues such as How Come You Do Me Like You Do, St. Louis, Memphis and Beale Street Blues.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Solo length: a chorus is a story
segments.summary: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination and likes two choruses on short pieces and ballads.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: Ballad playing on trombone and Goodbye Rose
segments.summary: Ballad trombone existed early; he remembers a beautiful trombone solo on Goodbye Rose played by a man he cannot name.

segments.chapter: Tatum, sessions and bandsmen (repeated passages)
segments.title: An old Arthur Pryor record and his Vanguard 78s
segments.summary: Dickenson shows Morgenstern an old record by a military bandleader and his original Vanguard 78s including Sleepy Time.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Tired of one-nighters and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: They discuss the one-nighter tours that wore him down and the band's need for a steady gig.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Young players coming up: Warren Vache
segments.summary: Young players should get road experience; he predicts the not-yet-20 Warren Vache will be one of the good ones.

segments.title: An old record by Arthur Pryor's band and the Vanguard 78s
segments.summary: Dickenson finds a record of a military bandleader and shows his original Vanguard 78s.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Tired of one-nighters and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: He enjoyed the band and hopes it gets a steady gig.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Young players coming up
segments.summary: Young players should get road experience; he predicts a not-yet-20 player will be one of the big ones.

segments.summary: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were marches jazzed up with syncopation, different from ragtime.

segments.title: What bands played when he started: songs and blues
segments.summary: Early bands played songs like Japanese Sandman and the blues, including How Come You Do Me Like You Do.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Solo length: a chorus is a story
segments.summary: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: Ballad playing on trombone and Goodbye Rose
segments.summary: Ballad trombone existed early; he remembers a beautiful trombone solo on Goodbye Rose by a man he cannot name.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, blues and ballads (repeated passages)
segments.title: An old record by Arthur Frye's band and the Vanguard 78s
segments.summary: Dickenson will find a record of a military bandleader and shows his original Vanguard 78s, including Sleepy Time.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: The Vanguard record and Sleepy Time Down South
segments.summary: They look at a ten-inch reissued record on which Dickenson sings Sleepy Time Down South, and a new tape starts with music.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: An old trombone ballad record and the circus-instrument myth
segments.summary: They listen to a c. 1910 record with a remarkable trombone ballad solo, and Morgenstern says it is wrong that the trombone was a circus instrument before jazz players got hold of it.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: His 1956 French Columbia record released only in England
segments.summary: Dickenson shows a rare record made in 1956 and released in England, including one of his own numbers, What Have You Done With the Key to Your Heart.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Preparing for record dates and learning the chords
segments.summary: He recorded the tune once before with little arrangement; record dates often give too little time to learn a solo, and knowing chords and melody is important.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: His songs and the singers who never recorded them
segments.summary: He has written many tunes, handed copies to people who never performed them, and would like Johnny Hodges to play some.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Near-misses joining the Ellington band
segments.summary: Duke Ellington heard him at a jam session in Indianapolis and later asked him to join when Lawrence Brown was leaving, but Brown stayed.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Travelling with the World's Greatest Jazz Band and Duke's schedule
segments.summary: He compares the World's Greatest Jazz Band's travelling with Duke Ellington's and discusses Billy Butterfield's bus rides and Harry Carney.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Wishing he had played with Louis Armstrong's band
segments.summary: Morgenstern says he could have seen Dickenson with Louis after Charlie left; they mention Big Chief Moore.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Jack Teagarden in Kansas City and Teagarden-style trombone
segments.summary: He met Teagarden at a Kansas City jam, remembers his Dinah solo, and agrees he and Jimmy Harrison both came from Louis.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Working with Fats Waller and Clarence Page in Cincinnati
segments.summary: Fats Waller did a radio show and used Clarence Page's band for outside work, with Una Mae Carlisle also in the band; Dickenson found Fats fun to work with.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Humiliation and violence on the road in the South in the Thirties
segments.summary: He tells of a bus stop in Georgia where women were refused a restroom, a sheriff fined the band for no reason, and a beating of a black man he witnessed, saying this is why he avoided the South.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Returning South with Claude Hopkins
segments.summary: He went South again with Claude Hopkins without incident like that, enjoyed the band, and says Fred Norman did most of the writing.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: His first record: the vocal with Luis Russell and microphone fright
segments.summary: John Nesbitt took him to the session; he was uncredited and nervous, has always feared microphones but likes a megaphone.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Sitting in at sessions and how it has become harder
segments.summary: Sitting in has gone on since the music began; now players ask whether you can play, and standards rose after the early Thirties.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Musicians learning in Army bands and the G.I. Bill
segments.summary: Many musicians learned more by joining Army bands and music schools during the war and under the G.I. Bill.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Dizzy and Charlie Parker at Monroe's Uptown House
segments.summary: He lived above Monroe's Uptown House, heard Dizzy and Parker through the floor, jammed with them and tried to adjust to their fast different style.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: The Bebop versus Dixieland split and the role of disc jockeys and the press
segments.summary: He thinks the split between Moldy Figs and Bebop came from disc jockeys and the press, not musicians, who are all friends.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Jam sessions as exchanging ideas
segments.summary: Sessions let players learn what others were doing and trade ideas, like a seminar, and are now rare.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Disc jockeys playing one thing over and over
segments.summary: He says radio programmers plug one kind of music and should give variety, which benefits advertisers too.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Remote band broadcasts from the Cotton Club and Roseland
segments.summary: He wishes bands were again broadcast live from clubs and hotels as in the old days.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Variety in radio: country, rock and roll and the rest
segments.summary: Country and rock are fine but he objects to hearing one type constantly and wishes radio gave variety.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Speed Webb broadcast locally but never recorded
segments.summary: Speed Webb's band broadcast locally but never made records or came to New York, which is why it was not a success.

segments.chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
segments.title: Coming to New York, McKinney's Cotton Pickers and Don Redman
segments.summary: Bands were not made until they came to New York; McKinney's Cotton Pickers came to record, and Don Redman wrote many songs.
